newsitem.title: USA: Carnegie buys disputed New Jersey bonds.
newsitem.headline: Carnegie buys disputed New Jersey bonds.

text.p: Carnegie Bank NA has purchased a controversial Little Egg Harbor, N.J., bond deal that prompted a rare boycott of the city's bond offering last month, an adviser to Carnegie told Reuters Wednesday.

John Kraft, counsel to Carnegie and an attorney with Lowenstein Sandler Kohl Fisher & Boylan, said the bank purchased $7.17 million of Little Egg Harbor Board of Education bonds in a deal set to close on Friday.

Little Egg tried to sell the bonds in a competitive offering last month, but failed to receive a single bid on its debt. Market participants said they were angry over the town's use of a disputed method of calling a previous certificates of participation issue, and wanted to send a message.
The controversy centers on Little Egg's use in April 1996 of a condemnation procedure that it said allowed it to redeem the COPs early, presenting holders of the debt with an unexpected call.
Kraft said while he does not believe the condemnation move was legal, it would not affect the current bond offering, which will be used to pay off notes tied to the former COPs issue.
"(Condemnation) gives the Board of Education a unilateral par call at its option," Kraft said. "I don't think that's a procedure that should be employed and I don't think ultimately it's legal."

Steve Terhune, the district's business administrator, declined to comment. It was unclear whether the move to a negotiated sale from a competitive offering would cost the district more money. Phillip Gentile, bond counsel to the district, was not available for comment.
New Jersey bond issuers are required to use competitive bidding on this type of bond issue, but Kraft said because of the market boycott the issue is permitted to be sold through negotiation.
In light of the market's snub, Carnegie hired Kraft to make sure there would be no legal problems with the bonds down the road, Kraft said.

The Little Egg controversy is one of several heating up around the issue of condemnation. Harmony, N.J., and Pinelands, N.J., both have used the procedure for school district debt issues as well, eliciting similar outrage among market participants who say the method of calling the debt early is simply a way to disavow legitimate debt.
Although Little Egg's use of the method last April pre-dates the other two examples, market participants reacted with even more fury against Harmony, filing lawsuits against the issuer.
Pinelands faced a market boycott when it tried to sell a $9 million deal in January.
